When interpreting language such as used in this study, it's important to remember that science defines male and female in terms of the metabolic cost of the germ cell. The 'male' of this species did not necessarily evolve from male ancestors, nor did the female necessarily evolve from female ancestors. You may have noted that these 'male' and 'female' insects have little in common with the sexual dimorphism of other species.

One could just as easily reverse the sexual distinction. In that case, instead of noting that the female sports a penetrating organ, one would note that, in this species, the male produces larger and fewer germ cells.

It is, on a case by case basis, perhaps a more valid categorization. But the only used definition of sex is germ cell size. Which is why one always has to view such language as potentially inapt or distorted.

The sperm cells are likely the usual size. It is the accompanying material that is large.

And female is defined as the place where the gametes merge. Many plants, for instance, have female gametes that are not especially large.
